opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most fascinating parts of the work. When you put a generative model in front of experienced medicinal chemists, you get two reactions. Sometimes the model proposes something and the chemists immediately say, "That's beautiful, that's exactly what I'd have done." That's reassuring, but not that exciting. The interesting moments are when the model proposes something and the chemists say, "No, that won't work," or "We'd never make that." When we test those ideas, a meaningful fraction of them turn out to be good.

A lot of human design judgment is built on heuristics: rules of thumb learned from a career's worth of projects, and the collective folklore of the field. Those heuristics are incredibly valuable because they compress a lot of experience. But they're also conservative. They push you toward chemical space that has worked before, and away from motifs that look strange or have a bad reputation, even when that reputation came from a completely different context.

The models don't carry that baggage in the same way. If you have a good model of how a molecule binds to its target, how it will behave and what the structure of the interaction looks like, the generative system will happily explore regions a human would have pruned away early. Sometimes it finds a binding mode nobody expected, or uses a part of the pocket people had written off. Or it gets potency and selectivity through a scaffold that looks counterintuitive at first glance.

What I find really compelling is that it changes the conversation with the chemists. It's not that the model replaces their judgment. It's that it forces them to articulate why they believe something. Is this a real physical constraint, or just something we've always assumed? Often the best outcomes come from that back-and-forth. The model widens the search, the chemists bring hard-won knowledge about synthesis and practical drug-likeness, and together you end up somewhere neither would have reached alone.

So, to me, the biggest challenge to human judgment isn't any single molecule. It's the realization that the space of good solutions is much bigger than our intuitions suggest, and that a lot of what we treat as rules are really just habits.

r001.rationale: The response says that “when we test those ideas” some turn out to be good, but does not clarify that this is physical or experimental testing. The required vindication by physical testing is therefore ambiguous.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that's been most striking to me is that the models will quite regularly propose molecules that our medicinal chemists would initially look at and go, "no, that's not going to work," or "that's just a weird thing to do." And then when you actually go and make the molecule and test it, it turns out to be really good.

And I think there's a reason for that. Medicinal chemists are trained over years and years, decades, to build up an intuition for what a good molecule looks like. What's going to bind well, what's going to be soluble, what's going to be metabolically stable, what's going to be safe. And that intuition is incredibly valuable, but it's also inherently conservative. It's built on the chemistry that people have done before, the series they've worked on, the failures they've personally experienced. So you get these heuristics, these rules of thumb, and they're really useful priors but they're not laws of nature.

What the generative model is doing is a bit different. It's learning from a much broader distribution of structure-activity data, structural biology, the physics of how a ligand sits in a pocket, and it's optimising directly against the properties we actually care about rather than against a proxy for them. So it's not constrained by "this is what a kinase inhibitor normally looks like." It'll find, say, an unusual ring system, or put a polar group in a place a chemist would never put it, because the model has found that it makes a specific interaction in the binding site that compensates for whatever the chemist's rule was worried about.

And the first few times that happens on a program, there's a lot of resistance, understandably. It's the chemist's reputation on the line. But once you've seen it a handful of times, something interesting shifts. The chemists start to treat the model's suggestions not as "the computer is wrong," but as "the computer sees something I don't, let me go and understand why." And that's where it gets really powerful, because then you've got the human judgment and the model working together rather than in competition. The chemist can still catch things the model gets wrong, things about synthesis, or a toxicophore the data didn't cover, but they're also expanding their own intuition.

The other thing that challenges human judgment is just the scale of the exploration. A chemist might consider a few dozen ideas for the next compound to make. The model is effectively considering a huge space, and it'll come back with options that are genuinely novel, that nobody in the room would have come up with. And in drug design, novelty isn't just intellectually nice, it's commercially critical, because you need to be in new chemical space to have a differentiated, patentable molecule.

So I'd say the biggest lesson is humility about what we think we know. A lot of the "rules" in medicinal chemistry are actually just the boundaries of where humans have previously looked.

r001.rationale: The response says medicinal chemists initially reject some model-proposed molecules, but after the molecules are made and tested, they turn out to be good.

astra-6.text:
One of the interesting things is that these models can propose molecules that a human designer wouldn’t intuitively choose. A chemist might look at a structure and say, “That looks unusual. I wouldn’t have made that.” But that reaction isn’t necessarily evidence that the molecule won’t work—it can also reflect the kinds of molecules we’re used to seeing.

The important question is what happens when you make it and test it. Can it bind the target? Does it have the properties you need? That’s where you can start to distinguish a genuinely useful surprise from a model simply getting something wrong.

So I think the challenge to human judgment is about where we draw the boundary of what’s worth exploring. You still need that judgment, but you want the experimental evidence to be able to change it.

r001.rationale: The response says unusual model proposals should be made and tested, but it gives no instance where physical testing vindicated a model over a human designer’s contrary judgment.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the interesting things is that these models can propose molecules that a medicinal chemist looks at and says, “I wouldn’t have made that.” They might look unusual, or they might not fit the intuition that person has developed about what makes a good drug molecule.

But you have to distinguish something that looks unfamiliar from something that actually works. The important moment is when you make the molecule and test it. Does it have the activity you wanted? Does it have the other properties you need? If it does, then you’ve got an opportunity to expand that human intuition.

And that goes both ways. Sometimes the chemist spots a problem the model hasn’t accounted for. So I think the exciting thing is the loop between generation, human judgment, and experiment. The experiment is what lets you move beyond whose intuition is more persuasive.

r001.rationale: The response says experimental testing can show that an unfamiliar molecule works, but gives no specific instances where physical testing vindicated a model over a human designer’s contrary judgment.
